basis: Letter prepared by Albert Browne with 'bursts of indignation dictated by the Governor' in reply to Senator Wilson's complaint, mid May 1861 (after Howe's report of 7 May, exact date not printed), Pearson v1 p219-220: 'His Excellency requests that you will not misconstrue his motives in expressing himself with this warmth of feeling ... but he does mean to express the indignant surprise with which he perceives that other States received at the hands of the Federal Government more consideration than Massachusetts' and he 'is even denied by the Secretary of War permission to clean Fort Warren at the expense of the State'. Shows a readiness to rebuke the War Department, not contempt for superiors as such: weak. Date approximate.

No document before 5 March 1861 in which Andrew speaks of Butler. Pearson v1 p183-185 (Butler 'a Breckinridge Democrat' who 'ran against Andrew for Governor') is Pearson's narrative of 16 Apr 1861, after the boundary, and the old cite p217 (Hoar to Andrew, May 1861) is after it too. Searched: the whole of Pearson v1 for Butler (every hit is after 15 Apr 1861).

Pearson v1 p96-97 says Andrew wrote 'straightway' to Montgomery Blair in Oct 1859 asking him to act for John Brown, and p134 lists Blair among the Washington advisers of Dec 1860, but neither prints a word of Andrew's about Blair, so neither is a document of regard. The letters that do show warmth (the introduction of April 1861, the 'personal friend' letter at p224) are after 5 March 1861.

Searched: N&H v3 p351-352 (Lincoln's reasons, but 'in every way qualified' is N&H's own 1890 phrase, not a document), the Chicago proceedings (CHI-1860 p109: Bates put in nomination, 48 votes on the first ballot, a measure of standing not of competence), NYT 17 and 18 Dec 1860 (OCR unreadable on Bates). Bates's own memorandum of 29 Mar 1861 (N&H v3 p432) is his advice, whose quality is our judgment and no contemporary one. No third-party contemporary judgment of his ability found.

Cabinet opinion of 16 Mar 1861 as quoted by N&H from the MS (v3 p388): 'True, war already exists by the act of South Carolina - but this Government has thus far magnanimously forborne to retort the outrage. And I am willing to forbear yet longer in the hope of a peaceful solution of our present difficulties.' Memorandum of 29 Mar 1861 (v3 p432): 'It is my decided opinion that Fort Pickens and Key West ought to be reenforced and supplied, so as to look down opposition at all hazards' but 'As to Fort Sumter - I think the time is come either to evacuate or relieve it.' Cautious on Sumter, firm on Pickens: mixed, so average. N&H print the documents of the time (Lincoln's secretaries, own side).

Bates's diary, quoted by N&H from the MS (v3 p351), on Lincoln's offer to come to St Louis: 'I thought I saw an unfitness in his coming to me, and that I ought to go to him' (entry about 13 Dec 1860, he went to Springfield on 15 Dec). A diary written at the time: courteous and deferential to the president-elect, co-operative but formal. Average. Read only as printed by N&H, since the 1933 edition is not public domain.

The Bates-Blair split in the sources is of May 1861 (N&H v4 p216: Lyon's friends found 'a ready advocate in Mr. Blair', Harney's friends 'in Mr. Bates'), N&H's narrative and after the boundary. The one pre-boundary document is weakly the other way: at Chicago on 18 May 1860 'Mr. Blair, of Missouri: I am commissioned by the representatives of the State of Missouri to present to this Convention the name of Edward Bates' (CHI-1860 p109). No document of Bates on Montgomery Blair before 5 March 1861 found.
